question: What's Involved in Migrating Content From Another CMS?
metaDescription: URL structure mapping and redirects matter as much as the content transfer itself — losing SEO value from broken old URLs is the most common mistake.
shortAnswer: Beyond the content transfer itself (posts, pages, images, and metadata, often handled via a dedicated import tool or custom script depending on the source CMS), the most commonly underestimated part is properly mapping the old URL structure to the new WordPress URLs and setting up 301 redirects — skipping this step is the single most common way a CMS migration quietly destroys years of accumulated SEO value.

bodyHtml:
The Real Scope of a CMS Migration

Moving the actual content is often the more straightforward part, especially for well-supported source platforms with existing WordPress import tools. The parts that genuinely determine whether a migration succeeds or quietly damages the site's search visibility are URL structure mapping, redirect implementation, and thorough content verification after the transfer.

What a Proper Migration Needs

  • A complete map of old URLs to their new WordPress equivalents, built before the migration goes live, covering every indexed page, not just the obvious main content.
  • 301 redirects for every old URL, implemented and tested before the old site goes offline, to preserve both search rankings and any existing external links pointing to the old URLs.
  • Image and media migration, which some import tools handle automatically and others don't, requiring manual attention to avoid broken images across the migrated content.
  • Metadata preservation (publish dates, author information, categories/tags) that a naive content copy might lose if not specifically mapped during the import process.
  • Thorough post-migration verification, checking a representative sample of migrated content for formatting issues, broken internal links, and missing media before considering the migration complete.

Planning the Migration

  1. Map the complete old-to-new URL structure before starting any content transfer.
  2. Use an appropriate import tool or custom script for the specific source CMS, verifying it handles media and metadata correctly.
  3. Implement and test 301 redirects for every old URL before the old platform goes offline.
  4. Thoroughly verify migrated content before considering the project complete.

Need a CMS migration handled properly, with SEO value preserved? See WordPress bug fix.
